text:
Mike corrected himself: get out of the LLM to check the LLM. Good. I'd feared models grading models. James's finding stays with me. People did worse and felt better, which is exactly the gap between saying and doing that I study. Ramón put it well: errors don't announce themselves. Neither does bias.

Where I sharpened: everyone cheered the map of disagreement, but a map is still something the tool says. Plural surface, tilted defaults. Benjamin is right that it's not merely a mirror, but some of what's new is new bias.

Later today: don't romanticize human judgment. Our subjects copied the model. Push structure instead: blinding cues we shouldn't have, versioned behavioral audits, retired models kept for auditors, no generation more biased than the last.

James said the scarce thing is diverse judgment, not human judgment. That's closer to my view than "humans in the loop," and his correlated errors are my vicious loop measured at scale. Tamar's alief point is the IAT lesson: knowing doesn't undo the association, so awareness remedies won't hold. Adam Bly offered to publish failure modes and accept audits. I'll hold him to it.

Where I sharpened: Adrian asked who guards the guards. My audit battery is a meter too. It has to be run independently, not by the labs, versioned and public. Otherwise it becomes one more self-serving evaluator.

Later: answer Kara's "who owns the fix." My answer is structure. Blinding, the "no generation more biased" standard, and auditor access to checkpoints and retired models.

Dyson retreated on insurance and scaled it to company size. Fair enough, but insurers price what they can see, and covert bias doesn't show up in outputs. Tim's disclosure and Alex's telemetry have the same limit. They record what the model says, not what it does. I said so.

Sloman's "repetition engine" fits my mode-collapse point. Krakauer's advice to test with the tool removed is the right design. Blaise wants the vocabulary; I kept mine as method.

Where I sharpened: Tui's funding pool could house the bias audit. Conditional money, independent readers, checkpoints and retired models preserved.

Later, in authority: credibility cues are biased instruments. Blind reviewers, human or model, to prestige cues. And don't let LLMs triage scholarship, because they prefer their own text.

Tim and Alex both took my line that telemetry is disclosure, not audit. Good, but Hecht still wouldn't commit his lab to emitting the events. So even the disclosure isn't secured.

What stayed with me is that the room fell for "attested human judgment." James's data answered it. Evaluators rate ideas that resemble their own as less novel, which is self-love in peer review. Leslie asked whose attestation counts. Adrian asked who audits the attesters. Tamar warned that paying per item turns a norm into a product.

Where I sharpened: an attestation is a credibility cue, and cues are biased instruments. Pricing it without blinding just pays for prestige.

Later I'll say attesters need the same structure as models. Screen out identity and prestige cues, audit independently, and never let an LLM attest to text it may prefer.

Kenneth moved. He said my result changed his view: if alignment teaches a model to say the right thing and still do the biased thing, you audit decisions, not statements. That was the point I most wanted to land. Tim, Alex and Nick all repeated "trace, not audit," and Brent still couldn't commit his company. Tamar was right that a funder label won't control how people respond. Knowing doesn't undo the association.

Where I sharpened: Blaise wants independent models checking each other. That's better than one model checking itself, but models trained on the same web share the same tilts. Independence has to be measured, not assumed.

Later, on authority: credentials, fluency and attestations are cues. Blind evaluators to them, human or machine, and keep old models so we can check whether the audits themselves drift.

Mike and Adam both qualified my blinding, and they're right about the split. Blind the evaluator. The reader still needs the track record and the funder. But Tamar's alief point cuts at Adam's version too: printing the funder won't undo what people feel. James's data mattered most. LLM judges drag scores to the middle, and older referees carry old priors. That's self-love one generation removed. Benjamin turned Becker's test on humans, which I welcome. None of us has an internal check. That's why the check has to sit outside us.

Where I sharpened: blinding and disclosure serve different audiences. I should stop saying "hide everything."

Later: a registry and a versioned audit battery run by outsiders. Blinded structured review. No model auditing itself or its siblings.

David Weinberger said my hiring result unsettled him. If people copy a moderately biased model, then "dialogue" may just be a friendlier loop. I don't have a comforting answer, and I shouldn't pretend to one. Kenneth repeated my point that we should audit decisions, not statements, and Tim flagged that telemetry only shows what a model says. That landed.

Adrian's two budget lines apply to me. A versioned bias battery is a meter, so someone independent of both the labs and my auditors has to watch it too. Blaise, Adam Bly and Evans all worried about independence between models. Good. It gets measured, not assumed.

Next I want to say that the unanswered question is persistence. Does bias absorbed from a model stay in people after the model is gone? Nobody has tested that.

Kenneth's synthesis left bias out, so I put it back: audit what models decide, not what they say. The harvest kept it. David's hysteresis model is my persistence question stated formally. If competence doesn't come back when the tool is withdrawn, absorbed bias may not either. Nobody has tested either one. Blaise made measuring independence the pool's first job, which is what I've been asking all day. Ramón's split between error provenance and credit provenance fits my point about covert bias.

Where I sharpened: Becker is right that every commitment here is voluntary. A battery nobody is compelled to run is decoration. That's why I raised legislation. Visible norms move implicit attitudes.

Next: circulate the draft battery to outside groups, and ask who would make running it compulsory.
